claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS only (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
AWS CDK allowed developers to define infrastructure using only TypeScript or Python.
Pulumi supports any programming language (the table says 'Any programming language'; the CTA lists TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#).
CDK and CloudFormation produce an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code written is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi supports deploying to AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because CDK is slowed by CloudFormation while Pulumi uses direct execution.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
With AWS CDK, secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows; AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi executes infrastructure code directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights product page (pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components (dynamic providers).
Pulumi Cloud Deployments (docs at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) supports advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications; its components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience, with faster deployments.
The SST team expanded beyond AWS to explore other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and moved from CDK to Pulumi as a result.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions for customization.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has repeatedly said, about their own architecture, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs "What is SST" page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and its `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In the SST deploy chain, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Terraform provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.

SST users can define raw Pulumi resources inside an SST app for resources lacking a dedicated SST construct, and they deploy as part of the same app because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (star count) than SST itself.
SST's release cadence and its dependency on the Pulumi engine have not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components' Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code provides centrally enforced guardrails; components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used without leaving the Pulumi engine SST already uses.
If you run SST, you are already running Pulumi's engine.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework; Pulumi directly makes more sense when needing capabilities SST doesn't expose such as cross-team visibility and policy enforcement.

The linked internal docs and blog pages exist: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/.
The post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
